content: 1. There was no observed effect of wall-to-wall carpeting or insulation on the incidence of cough or wheeze. Similarly, double-glazing did not show any impact on wheezing. The study had a medium level of directness and precision, with a low risk of bias for the study type. However, self-reported insulation data carried a high risk of bias. 2. The study by Breysse et al. (2015) focused on self-reported health outcomes associated with green-renovated public housing, primarily among elderly residents. The findings were based on an abstract only, and the study was included in a systematic review on insulation for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines. 3. Grey et al. (2017) conducted a controlled before-and-after study to assess the short-term health and psychosocial impacts of domestic energy efficiency investments in low-income areas. The study found some risk of bias due to incomplete follow-up. Improvements in mental and respiratory health were observed with certain interventions, but the precision of the results was unclear. 4. Homøe et al. (1999) investigated acute otitis media and sociomedical risk factors among unselected children in Greenland. The study found no association between self-reported insulation and episodes of acute otitis media. The indirect measure of insulation and unclear precision limited the study's conclusions. 5. Iversen et al. (1986) examined health and comfort changes among tenants after retrofitting their housing in Denmark. The study reported reductions in eye irritation and dry throat, but these findings did not reach statistical significance. Rheumatic symptoms and headaches were also reduced, but the results were not consistently significant. The study had a high risk of selection bias and insufficient information to assess precision. 6. Poortinga et al. (2017) analyzed social and health outcomes following upgrades to a national housing standard in Wales. Mental health improved with new windows, doors, loft, and external wall insulation but worsened with cavity wall insulation. Respiratory health showed similar patterns. General health improved with loft and external wall insulation but showed no association with new windows and doors, and worsened with cavity wall insulation. The study had some risk of bias due to self-reported health status and unclear confounding factors. 7. Tavernier et al. (2006) conducted the IPEADAM study, which examined indoor endotoxin exposure, family status, and housing characteristics in English children. The study found no difference in asthma prevalence between asthmatic and healthy children based on glazing systems. The precision of the results could not be measured, and there was some risk of bias due to high non-participation rates. 8. Telfar Barnard et al. (2011) evaluated the impact of retrofitted insulation and new heaters on health service utilization, pharmaceutical costs, and mortality in New Zealand. The study found no significant effect on hospitalizations or pharmaceutical prescriptions across various categories. The study had some risk of bias in control selection and health measurement, with imprecise results due to wide confidence intervals. 9. Windle et al. (2006) investigated housing-related difficulties, housing tenure, and variations in health status among older people in Wales. The study was a retrospective cohort design and included adults aged 70 and older. The recruitment was conducted via a door-to-door census based on the electoral roll, with a 19% refusal rate.
